metaTitle: Why Your LinkedIn Photo Gets Cropped and How to Stop It
metaDescription: LinkedIn shows your profile photo inside a circle, so the corners of a square upload are always cut off. Here is how to compose a photo that survives the crop.

content:
Your LinkedIn photo gets cropped because LinkedIn shows it inside a circle, and a circle cannot hold the corners of a square. Whatever sits near the edges of your upload, whether that is the top of your head, your shoulders or a bit of text, gets clipped away. The fix is to compose the photo for the circle before you upload it, then use LinkedIn's crop and reposition tools to finish the job.

This guide explains why the crop happens, how to frame a photo that survives it, and what to do when you already have a photo that keeps losing its edges.

Why does your LinkedIn photo get cropped and how do you stop it?

LinkedIn takes your square upload and masks it to a circle wherever the photo appears small: next to comments, in search results, in message threads and in the feed. The circle touches the square at four points and discards everything outside it, which is roughly a fifth of the image. To stop losing the important parts, keep your face in the centre, leave space above your head, and start with a square image rather than a portrait or landscape shot.

What exactly does the circle cut off?

Picture a square with a circle drawn inside it, touching all four sides. The circle covers the middle of every edge but misses every corner, and those corners are where people put the things they care about least on purpose. The problem is that a badly framed headshot puts important things there by accident.

The usual casualties are the top of the head, which sits in the upper corners when the face is too high in the frame, and the shoulders, which sit in the lower corners. Anything with lettering near an edge, like a name badge or a slogan on a wall, is also gone. A wide shot fares worst of all, because the face becomes a small dot in the middle of a circle that is already small.

How should you compose a photo for the circular crop?

Compose for the circle, not the square. That means the photo should still make sense if you cover the corners with your thumbs, which is a quick test you can do on your phone before uploading.

  • Head and shoulders only. The frame should stop just below the shoulders. Any lower and your face shrinks to make room for a torso the circle will hide anyway.
  • Leave headroom. A little space above the hair keeps the top of your head out of the upper corners. Too much space and your face drifts toward the bottom edge instead.
  • Face in the centre. Your eyes should sit slightly above the midpoint of the frame, with equal space either side. Off-centre framing looks stylish full size and lopsided in a circle.
  • Start square. A 1:1 source lets you control the crop. A portrait or landscape file forces LinkedIn to crop twice, once to a square and again to the circle.

If you are taking the photo yourself, step back a little further than feels natural and crop in afterwards. It is far easier to remove background than to add back a fringe that was never captured.

How do you use LinkedIn's crop and reposition tools?

LinkedIn lets you upload a photo, crop it, drag it to reposition, apply filters and choose who can see it, all from the intro section of your profile, as described on the LinkedIn Help page for adding and editing your profile photo. These tools are the second half of the fix. A well composed photo needs only a nudge, and a slightly off photo can often be rescued.

Open the editor, then zoom out until you see a little space around your head and drag the image so your eyes sit just above centre. Check the preview at the smallest size before saving. If the top of your head still touches the edge, zoom out a fraction more rather than dragging the photo down, which pushes your chin toward the bottom of the circle.

One caution: the tools can only work with what is in the file. If the original was taken too close, there is no headroom to reveal, and the honest fix is a new photo.

Why do the edges matter when the photo is so small?

Because the small version is the one that does the work. People decide how they feel about a face very quickly. Princeton research by Willis and Todorov found that judgements of trustworthiness and competence form after about 100 milliseconds of looking at a face, and that longer exposure mostly increases confidence rather than changing the verdict, as reported by Princeton University.

That snap judgement is made on the thumbnail beside your comment, not the full-size photo on your profile. A clipped forehead or a shoulder vanishing into the edge of the circle reads as careless at exactly the moment someone is forming a first impression.

What if you do not have a photo that fits?

You have three options: a photographer, a careful phone selfie, or an AI headshot. A photographer will frame for you but costs the most and takes the longest to book. A selfie is free, but getting headroom, centring and a square crop right on a phone at arm's length takes more attempts than most people expect.

Picturesk sits in between. You upload five to fifteen recent selfies, ten to twelve is the sweet spot, pick backgrounds and outfits, and we train a model on your face.

The finished set arrives by email in about an hour as square 1:1 headshots composed head and shoulders, which is exactly the framing that survives the circle. LinkedIn headshots from Picturesk start at $9 for five images, and if they do not look like you, you reply within 3 days for a full refund.

The AI headshot generator also screens your selfies before you pay, so a photo with sunglasses, a hat or a face too small in frame is flagged and can be swapped. That matters here, because the input photos follow the same rule as the output: one clear face, well centred, not crowding the edges.

faqs.question: Why does LinkedIn crop my profile photo into a circle?
faqs.answer: LinkedIn shows profile photos inside a circle wherever they appear small, such as beside comments, in search and in messages. A circle cannot contain the corners of a square, so those corners are always cut away. Anything near the edges of your upload, including the top of your head or your shoulders, is lost.

faqs.question: How do I stop LinkedIn cutting off the top of my head?
faqs.answer: Leave headroom. Frame the photo head and shoulders with a little space above your hair, and keep your eyes just above the centre of the frame. Then open LinkedIn's photo editor, zoom out slightly and reposition the image until the preview at the smallest size shows your whole head.

faqs.question: Should my LinkedIn photo be square before I upload it?
faqs.answer: Yes, a square 1:1 file gives you control over what ends up in the circle. A portrait or landscape photo has to be cropped to a square first, and then to the circle, so you lose more than you intended. Picturesk delivers every headshot square, composed head and shoulders, for this reason.

faqs.question: Can I fix a cropped LinkedIn photo without taking a new one?
faqs.answer: Often, yes. LinkedIn's editor lets you crop, zoom and reposition the photo from your profile intro section, which is enough when the face is only slightly off centre. If the original was taken too close and there is no headroom in the file, no amount of repositioning will add it back, and you need a new photo.
